# Why Quarto: literate programming

> *Treat programs as a "literature" understandable to **human beings**.*
> — Donald Knuth

An analysis is more than its code. Someone (a teammate, a reviewer, you in
three months) needs to know *why* each step happened and what the results mean.
A Quarto document (`.qmd`) weaves **prose, code, and the code's output** into one
file, then renders it to a finished HTML page, PDF, or Word doc. Change the data,
re-render, and every number and chart updates — nothing is copy-pasted by hand.

Every project deliverable this semester is a `.qmd`, so this is the format your
work gets graded in. To try it: open `quarto_demo.qmd` in Positron and click
**Preview**.

# Anatomy of a .qmd file

A `.qmd` has three parts: a **YAML header** (the settings), **markdown text**,
and **R code**.

## 1. The header

The header sits between two `---` lines at the very top of the file:

```yaml
---
title: Your title
author: Author name
toc: true
format:
  html:
    theme: united
---
```

| Setting | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| `format: html` | Web page (the default for our work) |
| `format: pdf` | PDF via LaTeX |
| `format: docx` | Microsoft Word |
| `toc: true` | Adds a table of contents |
| `theme: united` | Changes the HTML look |

No LaTeX for PDF output? Run `tinytex::install_tinytex()` once in R.

## 2. Markdown text

Bookmark [commonmark.org/help](https://commonmark.org/help/), and when you have
10 minutes, do its [tutorial](https://commonmark.org/help/tutorial/).

| Type this | To get |
|-----------|--------|
| `# Header 1` (up to six) | Section headers |
| `*italic*` or `_italic_` | *italic* |
| `**bold**` | **bold** |
| `~~strikethrough~~` | ~~strikethrough~~ |
| backticks around text | `code text` |
| a dash and a space | bulleted list item |
| `1.` and a space | numbered list item |
| `[Download R](http://r-project.org)` | [Download R](http://r-project.org) |

## 3. R code

**Inline code** runs inside a sentence: writing `` `r 3 + 4` `` in the text
prints *7* in the rendered document.

**Code chunks** start with three backticks and `{r}` on their own line and end
with three backticks. Positron's **Insert Code Cell** does this for you.
**Chunk options** go at the top of the chunk, each on a line starting with a
hash and a pipe:

| Option | Shows code? | Shows output? | Runs? |
|--------|-------------|---------------|-------|
| *(default)* | yes | yes | yes |
| `echo: false` | no | yes | yes |
| `eval: false` | yes | no | no |
| `include: false` | no | no | yes |

Also handy: `warning: false`, `message: false`, `fig-width`, `fig-height`. All
options are in the
[Quarto cell reference](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/cells/cells-knitr.html).

## The setup chunk

Make the first chunk a `setup` chunk with `include: false`. It sets global
options, loads libraries, and reads the data, so every later chunk can use them:

```r
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7.252,
  fig.height = 4
)

library(tidyverse)
bears <- read_csv(file.path('data', 'bear_killings.csv'))
```

A rendered `.qmd` starts from a **clean R session**. An object that exists only
in your console doesn't exist when you render. If the document needs it, create
it in a chunk.

## Putting it together

A complete, renderable `.qmd`, in the shape of the `bears.qmd` practice:

<!-- Built as a Typst raw block, not a markdown fence: knitr executes any line
     that starts with a chunk fence, even inside a code block. -->

```{=typst}
#raw(block: true, lang: "markdown", (
  "---",
  "title: \"Bears Analysis\"",
  "format: html",
  "---",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "#| label: setup",
  "#| include: false",
  "library(tidyverse)",
  "bears <- read_csv(file.path('data', 'bear_killings.csv'))",
  "```",
  "",
  "### Which months have the most bear killings?",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "bears %>%",
  "  count(month) %>%",
  "  arrange(desc(n))",
  "```",
).join("\n"))
```

`count(variable)` counts the rows for each unique value, the quickest way to
answer "which is more common?" Add `arrange(desc(n))` to put the largest first.

# Plotting with ggplot2

ggplot2 (Hadley Wickham, 2005) implements Leland Wilkinson's *Grammar of
Graphics*: a chart is built from **layers**, added one at a time with `+`.

| Layer | Function | Question it answers |
|-------|----------|---------------------|
| 1. Data | `ggplot()` | What data? |
| 2. Aesthetics | `aes()` | Which variables go where? |
| 3. Geometries | `geom_*()` | Points? Bars? Lines? |
| 4. Labels | `labs()` | What do the axes say? |
| 5. Theme | `theme_*()` | How does it look? |

| Aesthetic | Controls |
|-----------|----------|
| `x`, `y` | Position on the axes |
| `color` | Points, lines, and bar outlines |
| `fill` | Inside of bars and areas |
| `shape` | Point symbol (max 6 groups) |
| `size` | Point size or line width |
| `alpha` | Transparency, 0 to 1 |

Map any of these aesthetics to a variable inside `aes()`, or set it to a
constant outside `aes()`. A full chart, all five layers:

```r
mpg %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Engine displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway fuel economy (mpg)",
    title = "Larger engines are less fuel efficient"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Note the two different joiners: the pipe passes data *into* `ggplot()`; after
that, layers are joined with a plus sign.

## Mapping vs. setting

```{=typst}
#keypoint[
  *Inside `aes()` you map a variable; outside `aes()` you set a constant.*
  `geom_point(aes(color = class))` colors each point by its vehicle class.
  `geom_point(color = 'blue')` makes every point blue. Put a fixed value inside
  `aes()` and ggplot treats it as a one-level variable, not a color.
]
```

**Where to put `aes()`.** In `ggplot(aes(...))` the mapping applies to *every*
layer. Inside one geom, say `geom_point(aes(...))`, it applies to that layer
only, so a following `geom_line()` with no mapping errors out.

## The main geoms

| Geom | Makes | Notes |
|------|-------|-------|
| `geom_point()` | Scatterplot | Map `color` or `shape` |
| `geom_line()` | Connects dots, left to right | Messy on scattered data |
| `geom_smooth()` | Best-fit trend line | `se = FALSE` drops the band |
| `geom_col()` | Bars of a given height | Summarize first, e.g. `count()` |

**Points and lines use `color`; bars use `fill`.** `color` on a bar only outlines it.

## Bar chart recipe

```r
mpg %>%
  count(class, drv) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_col(
    aes(x = reorder(class, n), y = n, fill = drv),
    position = "dodge",  # side-by-side, not stacked
    width = 0.7
  )
```

- `count(class)` makes the summary data frame; a `fill` variable must be counted
  too, as in `count(class, drv)`.
- `reorder(class, n)` sorts bars by count instead of alphabetically.
- For many long category names, put them on the y axis to keep them readable.

## Facets

Too many colors to tell apart? Split the chart into small multiples:

| Code | Result |
|------|--------|
| `facet_wrap(~class)` | One panel per class |
| `facet_grid(drv ~ cyl)` | Rows by `drv`, columns by `cyl` |

## Themes

Built in: `theme_bw()`, `theme_minimal()`, `theme_classic()`, `theme_void()`.
More in the **ggthemes** package (`ggthemes::theme_economist()`) and
**hrbrthemes** (`hrbrthemes::theme_ipsum()`).

# Your project: defining attribute levels

Now that your attributes are in the Model Relationships Table, give each one
**levels**, the specific values respondents will see.

| Kind | Example levels |
|------|----------------|
| Continuous | Price: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (\$) |
| Continuous | Power output: 60, 80, 120 (W) |
| Discrete | Color: Red, Blue, Yellow |
| Discrete | Material: Plastic, Aluminum, Glass |

Look at competitors. Choose values that cover the full range on the market today,
and maybe some of the future.

# Conjoint survey components

Think of the survey as a **conversation**: add transition pages ("Great job!
Now we'll ask you about…") between sections.

| Part | Contents | Screen for |
|------|----------|------------|
| 1. Intro | Welcome, consent, eligibility | Target population |
| 2. Conjoint | Education, practice question, choices | Random answers |
| 3. Other | Critical info, demographics, finale | — |

- **Education pages** explain each attribute before the choices. Relative
  comparisons help: "1/2 lb, about 1 cup of water".
- **The practice question** doubles as an **attention check**.
- **After the choices**, you can also drop respondents who picked the same
  option every time.

# Errors you will hit this week

| Problem | Usual cause |
|---------|-------------|
| `object not found` on render | Created in console, not in a chunk |
| `could not find function "ggplot"` | No `library(tidyverse)` in setup |
| `cannot open file 'data/...'` | Folder not opened in Positron |
| Plot doesn't show the geom | Plus sign at the start of a line, not the end |
| Bars ignore the color | Used `color`; bars need `fill` |
| Every point is one odd color | Constant put inside `aes()` |
| `missing aesthetics: x and y` | `aes()` is only in another geom |
